subject: Martha of Bethany
note: Evidence for Martha's Bible figure page. A thin record (Luke 10:38-42; John 11; John 12:1-2), so a short page: five moments, no miracles section (the raising of Lazarus is Jesus' act and is told among the moments), no death section (Scripture says nothing of her end; the Provençal legend is a myth, named as later). Every quotation is in martha.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/martha/ (gitignored); Bible lines are from the Berean Standard Bible (shared/bsb-berean-standard-bible.txt; the chapters used are also copied to people/martha/bsb-martha-chapters.txt). The Fathers' texts on Martha and Mary were already on disk in sources/gregory-sources/martha-mary/ and are copied into people/martha/.

life.text: Martha is named only in Luke 10:38-42 and John 11 and 12; Matthew and Mark never name her.
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), "St. Martha": "Mentioned only in Luke 10:38-42 ; and John 11, 12, sqq." Checked against the BSB: no verse of Matthew or Mark contains "Martha".

life.text: Her home was Bethany, a little less than two miles from Jerusalem; Luke calls it only a village and says she welcomed Jesus into her home.
In His last week, Jesus went out to Bethany for the night.
life.source: Matthew 21:17 (BSB): "Then He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night." Mark 11:11.
life.note: The page does not claim He stayed in Martha's house.

life.text: Her sister was Mary and her brother Lazarus; Luke never mentions Lazarus; no parents, husband or children are named.
life.source: John 11:1-2, 19; Luke 10:38-42 (BSB). The Lazarus of Luke 16 is a different man, in a parable.
life.note: The Golden Legend names parents (Syro and Encharia) and says she never married: a medieval legend, not used as fact.

life.text: Her name is probably Aramaic, meaning mistress.
life.source: Bible Hub, Strong's Greek 3136: "Word Origin: [probably of Chaldee origin (meaning mistress)]"; "of Aramaic origin".

life.text: The name is found in a Nabataean inscription dated AD 5, found at Puteoli (near Naples).
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), "St. Martha": "The Aramaic form occurs in a Nabatæan inscription found at Puteoli, and now in the Naples Museum; it is dated A.D. 5 (Corpus Inscr. Semit., 158)".
life.note: Puteoli is modern Pozzuoli, beside Naples (common knowledge).

life.text: The moments: the visit and "Martha, Martha" (Luke 10:38-42); the message and the two days' wait (John 11:1-16); Martha meets Jesus, "I am the resurrection and the life", her confession (John 11:17-27); the tomb and Lazarus raised (John 11:28-44); the supper six days before the Passover, "Martha served" (John 12:1-11).
life.note: John 12 does not say whose house the supper was in: Chrysostom (Homily 65 on John) takes it to be Martha's, 'Some, however, say, that it took place in the house of another'; the Catholic Encyclopedia argues for Simon the leper's (Matthew 26:6; Mark 14:3). The page does not name the house.

life.text: Her confession (John 11:27) is close to Peter's (Matthew 16:16).
life.source: BSB: John 11:27 "I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world"; Matthew 16:16 "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God".
life.note: Used in kin (Peter), as a comparison of the two texts only.

life.text: John 11:5 names Martha first and does not name her sister: "Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus."
"Jesus wept" (John 11:35), the shortest verse in most English Bibles, is in her story.
life.note: Common knowledge for English Bibles; worded "most English Bibles" on purpose.

fathers.text: Augustine: both sisters good and loved; Martha the image of the present life, Mary of the life to come; the Lord did not blame Martha's work; the works of mercy end in heaven; "The repetition of the name is a token of love"; "the handmaid received her Lord".
fathers.source: Augustine, Sermons 103 and 104 (Benedictine numbering; NPNF1 6 Sermons 53 and 54 on the New Testament), tr. R. G. MacMullen, 1888.
fathers.note: The Episcopal calendar quotes Sermon 104 as "Martha has to set sail in order that Mary can remain quietly in port", from another translation; not in the NPNF text and not used.

fathers.text: Abba Moses (Cassian, Conference 1, chapter 8): the monk's main effort is that the soul cleave to God; Martha's service was no unworthy work, but the Lord makes the chief good contemplation.
fathers.source: John Cassian, Conferences 1.8, tr. Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF2 11, 1894.

fathers.text: Gregory the Great: Leah and Rachel as the active and contemplative lives; "Martha's concern is not reproved"; the active great, the contemplative far better.
fathers.source: Gregory the Great, Moralia, Book 6, chapter 37 (sections 60-61), Library of the Fathers, Oxford, 1844.

fathers.text: Chrysostom (Homily 44 on John): some abused Christ's words to live in idleness; Paul worked with his hands; the words to Martha concern knowing the right season. (Homily 62): Martha 'the weaker', her answer not understanding the whole meaning, yet the sisters 'truly wise as well as loving'.
fathers.source: John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of John 44 and 62, tr. G. T. Stupart, NPNF1 14 (shared/npnf114.txt).

fathers.text: Meister Eckhart (Sermon 86) argued Martha was the more mature sister; most premodern writers put Mary higher, but stressed the need for both vocations.
fathers.source: The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 29 July (shared/lff2022.txt).
fathers.note: Told in our words from LFF's summary; Eckhart not quoted (no public-domain translation fetched).

legend.text: The Golden Legend's Life of S. Martha: Martha, Mary, Lazarus, Maximin and others put in a ship without sail, oars or rudder, landing at Marseilles; the dragon between Arles and Avignon, tamed with holy water and the cross, bound with her girdle and killed by the people; Tarascon named after it; her death and burial at Tarascon.
legend.source: Jacobus de Voragine, The Golden Legend (compiled by 1275, per the Fordham edition's title page), Englished by William Caxton, 1483, ed. F. S. Ellis (Temple Classics, 1900), volume 4.
legend.note: Told on the page only as a medieval legend (myths); "compiled in the 1200s" covers both the 1260s dating in the brief and Fordham's 1275.

legend.text: The Orthodox tradition: after Stephen's death the sisters helped Lazarus proclaim the Gospel in various lands; they are also commemorated on the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearing Women.
legend.source: OCA, Righteous Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus (4 June).
legend.note: Paraphrased, not quoted (a modern text). The Sunday falls two weeks after Pascha (the third Sunday of Pascha): common knowledge.

legend.text: Tarascon's processional dragon is one of the processional giants and dragons of Belgium and France on UNESCO's Representative List (inscribed 2008, proclaimed 2005).
legend.source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, 'Processional giants and dragons in Belgium and France': "French towns (Cassel, Douai, Pézenas and Tarascon), where they remain living traditions".
legend.note: UNESCO does not name the Tarasque or Martha; the page says only that Tarascon carries the legend's dragon in procession.

legend.text: In art: Martha with the dragon and holy water (Cornelis Buys, about 1528; Correggio's Saints Peter, Martha, Mary Magdalen and Leonard, the Met; Charles-André van Loo, Tarascon; the Hôtel-Dieu de Beaune statue), and in the kitchen while Mary listens (Aertsen, Beuckelaer, Velázquez, Vermeer).
legend.source: Wikimedia Commons, files in Category:Paintings of Saint Martha and the 'Christ in the House of Martha and Mary' paintings found by search.
legend.note: The page's 'often' rests on these examples, not on a reference work.

feasts.text: Catholic: 29 July, Memorial of Saints Martha, Mary and Lazarus, since the decree of 26 January 2021; before that Martha alone.
feasts.source: USCCB Liturgical Calendar 2026 (shared/usccb-2026cal.txt): "29 Wed Saints Martha, Mary, and Lazarus". Congregation for Divine Worship, decree of 26 January 2021 (people/martha/vatican-2021-decree.txt): the Latin Church's uncertainty about Mary's identity "resulted in the inclusion of Martha alone on 29 July", now resolved; Pope Francis decreed the memorial of all three.
feasts.note: The decree is paraphrased, not quoted (a modern translation).

feasts.text: The Franciscans put Martha's feast in their calendar in 1262 on 29 July, the octave of Mary Magdalene; Rome received it by the end of the 1200s. The 1969 reform left Martha unchanged.
feasts.source: Calendarium Romanum (1969), 29 July: "Festum S. Marthae ascriptum est a Franciscanis in suo Calendario anno 1262, die 29 iulii celebrandum, i. e. in octava S. Mariae Magdalenae. Eodem saeculo xm exeunte, Romae receptum est." and "Quoad S. Martham nihil mutatur."

feasts.text: Roman Martyrology 1916, 29 July: at Tarascon, St Martha, hostess of our Saviour, sister of blessed Mary Magdalen and St Lazarus.
Church of England 29 July: Mary, Martha and Lazarus, Companions of Our Lord. Episcopal Church 29 July: Mary and Martha of Bethany. LCMS and ELCA 29 July: Mary, Martha, and Lazarus of Bethany.
feasts.note: The CofE's rank for the day (lesser festival or commemoration) was not read from the text file and is not claimed.

feasts.text: Orthodox: 4 June, Righteous Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus (OCA); also the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearing Women.
feasts.note: Old-calendar churches keep 4 June on 17 June (the 13-day difference, stated generally on the page).

pictures.what: Saint Martha in a landscape, Cornelis Jacobsz Buys IV, between 1528 and 1530, oil on wood, 60.5 x 49.5 cm (sold at Koller, Zurich; private collection).
pictures.size: original 4912 x 6000; saved 1474 x 1800 (light blur against panel crackle), 350 KB
pictures.note: She holds a holy-water sprinkler and bucket, with the Tarascon dragon's head at lower right.

pictures.what: The Raising of Lazarus, Novgorod school, about 1497, from the festal tier of the iconostasis of the Dormition Cathedral, Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery; the Russian Museum, St Petersburg. 71.5 x 58 cm.
pictures.note: The two women bowing at Christ's feet are the sisters, as in the standard iconography of the feast.

could_not_verify: Patronages (cooks, servants, housekeepers, innkeepers): no source fetched; left out.
Her tomb or relics shown at the collegiate church of Sainte-Marthe, Tarascon: not fetched; the page says only that the legend and the 1916 Martyrology place her there.
A Coptic commemoration: not found in the files on disk; left out.
Pope Gregory the Great's identification of Mary of Bethany with Mary Magdalene (Homily 33 on the Gospels): not fetched; the page says only 'the Latin Church', as the 2021 decree does.

checked: Number tiles against the BSB (Luke 10:41; John 11:17, 39; 12:1-2).

Feasts: 29 July in USCCB 2026, the CofE calendar (Mary, Martha and Lazarus, Companions of Our Lord), LFF 2022 (Mary and Martha of Bethany), LSB and ELCA (all three); the Calendarium Romanum's 1262 note; OCA 4 June.

Attributions: Chrysostom Homily 62 on John read in context; Augustine Sermons 103 and 104; Cassian, Conference 1; Gregory's Moralia; LFF 2022's summary of Eckhart's Sermon 86 (the page retells, does not quote); the Golden Legend's voyage, dragon and Tarascon lines; the 1916 Martyrology's 29 July line read in the scan; the Catholic Encyclopedia on the Puteoli inscription.

The dragon told as a medieval legend with its source and date; the Mary Magdalene question in each side's terms; both pictures' licences on their Commons pages (PD-art|PD-old-auto-expired and PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired).
changed: Feast note: 'eight days after Mary Magdalene's' became 'a week after Mary Magdalene's'. The Calendarium says 'in octava', the octave day: 29 July is seven days after 22 July.
What others said: Chrysostom's line is about her answer to 'Do you believe this?' (her confession, John 11:27), so the 'who' now says so instead of 'her answer on the road'.
left_for_owner: The band shows the Tarascon dragon and holy water, which come from the legend, not the Gospels.
Chrysostom's less flattering reading sits beside Augustine's warmer one; the myth 'Jesus told Martha off' overlaps the 'Two sisters' section.
'Jesus wept' as the shortest verse in most English Bibles rests on common knowledge, with no source fetched.
